records.source: בְּ֭רִית כָּרַ֣תִּי לְעֵינָ֑י וּמָ֥ה אֶ֝תְבּוֹנֵ֗ן עַל־בְּתוּלָֽה׃
records.gloss: A covenant I made with my eyes; and how would I look closely at a virgin?
pieces: I made a covenant with my eyes; \q how then could I look with desire at a young woman?

L.1: A covenant I made with my eyes; \q how then would I gaze at a virgin?

R.1: I made a solemn agreement with my eyes. \q So how could I look at a young woman with desire?

decisions.choice: the start of Job's oath of innocence, the last part of the speech begun in 29:1
decisions.reason: Chapter 31 closes the speech Job began in 29:1, where he looked back on his past (chapter 29) and his present shame (chapter 30). Here he swears that he is innocent, sin by sin, in a long chain of "if I have done this, let that happen to me" (verses 5-40). After it the friends say nothing more, and Elihu speaks (32:1-6).

decisions.choice: made a covenant with my eyes: bound himself by a solemn commitment about what he would look at
decisions.reason: To "cut a covenant" is to make a binding agreement. Job speaks as if he had made one with his own eyes: they are bound not to look where they should not. Job begins with the eyes because desire starts there (verse 7).

decisions.choice: look closely: gaze at with desire
decisions.reason: The verb (bin, in a form meaning to look carefully, to consider) here means a lingering look with desire, the look that leads to the sin of verse 9.

decisions.choice: a virgin: a young woman of marriageable age who is not married
decisions.reason: The word (betulah) names a young unmarried woman, one who would normally be a virgin (Deuteronomy 22:19). The point is not her virginity but that Job did not let himself look at any woman who was not his wife with desire.

decisions.choice: look with desire at a young woman
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the look is (m3) and use "young woman" (m4), since "virgin" in English draws attention to sexual history rather than to the woman's age and unmarried state. Literal keeps "virgin".

records.heading: A covenant with my eyes

records.source: וּמֶ֤ה׀חֵ֣לֶק אֱל֣וֹהַּ מִמָּ֑עַל וְֽנַחֲלַ֥ת שַׁ֝דַּ֗י מִמְּרֹמִֽים׃
records.gloss: And what [is the] portion of God from above, and [the] inheritance of Shaddai from [the] heights?
pieces: For what portion does God above assign, \q what inheritance does the Almighty give from on high?

L.2: And what [is the] portion from God above, \q and [the] inheritance from the Almighty on high?

R.2: What does God in heaven give to someone who does that? \q What does God All-Powerful hand out from on high?

decisions.choice: portion of God: the lot God hands out to the person who sins
decisions.reason: "The portion of God" is what God allots, and verse 3 gives the answer: ruin for the wicked. Zophar and Job both used the same pair of words for the fate of the wicked (20:29; 27:13). Job does not deny the teaching; he swears that it does not apply to him.

decisions.choice: God ('Eloah) and the Almighty (Shaddai)
decisions.reason: Job uses 'Eloah, rendered "God", and Shaddai, rendered "the Almighty" (see 5:17).

decisions.choice: from above, from the heights: from heaven
decisions.reason: "Above" and "the heights" are places where God is (16:19; 25:2): the lot is assigned from heaven.

decisions.choice: to someone who does that
decisions.reason: Readable says who receives the portion: the person who sins as verse 1 describes (m1). It names Shaddai "God All-Powerful", as in every book.

records.source: הֲלֹא־אֵ֥יד לְעַוָּ֑ל וְ֝נֵ֗כֶר לְפֹ֣עֲלֵי אָֽוֶן׃
records.gloss: Not calamity for [the] unjust, and disaster for workers of wickedness?
pieces: Is it not ruin for the unrighteous, \q and disaster for those who do evil?

L.3: [Is it] not calamity for the unjust, \q and disaster for the workers of wickedness?

R.3: Surely it is ruin for people who are unjust, \q and disaster for those who do evil.

decisions.choice: a question that expects the answer yes
decisions.reason: "Is it not ...?" states what everyone in the debate agrees on: God sends ruin to the wicked (18:12; 21:30). This is why Job's oaths in the rest of the chapter are so serious: if he were guilty, he would be calling that ruin down on himself.

decisions.choice: calamity: sudden ruin
decisions.reason: The word ('eyd) is a crushing disaster, used of the end of the wicked (18:12; 21:17, 30). Verse 23 calls it "calamity from God".

decisions.choice: disaster: an unheard-of misfortune
decisions.reason: The word (nekher) is related to the word for "foreign, strange"; here it means a disaster out of the ordinary.

decisions.choice: Surely it is ...
decisions.reason: Readable turns the question into the statement it implies (m1), which is easier to follow.

records.source: הֲלֹא־ה֭וּאיִרְאֶ֣ה דְרָכָ֑י וְֽכָל־צְעָדַ֥י יִסְפּֽוֹר׃
records.gloss: Not he sees my ways, and all my steps he counts?
pieces: Does {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} not see my ways \q and count every step I take?

L.4: Does {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} not see my ways, \q and count all my steps?

R.4: Does God not see everything I do \q and count every step I take?

decisions.choice: he: God, stressed
decisions.reason: The pronoun is written out, which stresses it: God himself, the giver of the portion in verse 2. Job is about to swear his innocence before the one who sees everything (34:21).

decisions.choice: ways, steps: a person's conduct
decisions.reason: To see someone's ways and count their steps is to know everything they do. Job complained earlier that God counted his steps to find fault (14:16); here he welcomes it, since the count will show him innocent (verse 37).

decisions.choice: God; everything I do
decisions.reason: Readable names God for the pronoun and says what "my ways" means (m2).

records.source: אִם־הָלַ֥כְתִּי עִם־שָׁ֑וְא וַתַּ֖חַשׁ עַל־מִרְמָ֣ה רַגְלִֽי׃
records.gloss: If I have walked with falsehood, and has hurried to deceit my foot,
pieces: If I have walked with falsehood, \q or my foot has hurried after deceit,

L.5: If I have walked with falsehood, \q and my foot has hurried to deceit,

R.5: Have I lived a lie? \q Have I hurried to cheat others?

decisions.choice: if: the form of an oath; "if I have done this, let that happen to me"
decisions.reason: An oath in Hebrew names a wrong and then a curse on oneself: "if I have done X, let Y happen to me" (verses 7-8, 9-10, 21-22, 38-40; Psalm 7:4-6). Often the curse is left unspoken, and then "if" alone means "I swear I have not" (verses 29, 33), while "if not" means "I swear I have" (verses 20, 31, 36). Job is not wondering whether he did these things; he is putting himself under oath that he did not.

decisions.choice: falsehood, deceit: lying and cheating
decisions.reason: The first word (shav') means what is empty or false; the second (mirmah) is deceit, fraud. To "walk with" falsehood is to keep company with it, to live by it.

decisions.choice: the sentence goes on into verse 6
decisions.reason: Verse 6 either completes the oath ("let him weigh me") or breaks in with a wish before the next oath begins in verse 7. Either way, the oath of verse 5 is answered by God's judgment.

decisions.choice: questions in place of "if" clauses (throughout the chapter)
decisions.reason: Long chains of "if" clauses are hard to follow. Readable asks "Have I ...?" and then gives the curse with "If I have, then let ...". The sense is the same: Job swears he has not done these things (m1).

records.source: יִשְׁקְלֵ֥נִי בְמֹאזְנֵי־צֶ֑דֶק וְיֵדַ֥ע אֱ֝ל֗וֹהַּ תֻּמָּתִֽי׃
records.gloss: Let him weigh me in scales of righteousness, and let know God my integrity.
pieces: let {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} weigh me on honest scales, \q and let God know my integrity.

L.6: let {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} weigh me in scales of righteousness, \q and let God know my integrity.

R.6: Let God weigh me on honest scales. \q Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will know that I am blameless.

decisions.choice: scales of righteousness: honest, accurate scales
decisions.reason: The same phrase (mozne tsedeq) is used in the law for honest weights (Leviticus 19:36; Ezekiel 45:10). Job asks to be weighed fairly; he is sure the result will show him innocent.

decisions.choice: integrity: wholeness, blamelessness
decisions.reason: The word (tummah) is the one God used of Job (2:3), his wife threw at him (2:9), and Job swore to keep (27:5). It comes from the same root as "blameless" in 1:1.

decisions.choice: let God know: let God acknowledge
decisions.reason: "Know" here means to recognize and admit: Job wants God to see and confirm that he is innocent.

decisions.choice: honest scales
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "scales of righteousness" means (m1); Literal keeps the Hebrew phrase.

decisions.choice: that I am blameless
decisions.reason: Readable puts "integrity" as "blameless", the book's theme word of 1:1, from the same root (m2).

records.source: אִ֥ם תִּטֶּ֣ה אַשֻּׁרִי֮ מִנִּ֪י הַ֫דָּ֥רֶךְ וְאַחַ֣ר עֵ֭ינַי הָלַ֣ךְ לִבִּ֑י וּ֝בְכַפַּ֗י דָּ֣בַק מֻאֽוּם׃
records.gloss: If has turned aside my step from the way, and after my eyes has gone my heart, and to my hands has stuck a blemish,
pieces: If my steps have turned from the path, \q if my heart has followed my eyes, \q or if any stain has clung to my hands,

L.7: If my step has turned aside from the way, \q and my heart has gone after my eyes, \q and a blemish has stuck to my hands,

R.7: Have I left the right path? \q Has my heart gone after whatever my eyes wanted? \q Is there any stain of wrongdoing on my hands?

decisions.choice: the way: the path of right living God commands
decisions.reason: Job has already said, "I have kept his way and not turned aside" (23:11). To turn aside from the way is to leave a life of obedience.

decisions.choice: my heart has gone after my eyes: I let desire follow what I saw
decisions.reason: The heart is the seat of will and desire. To let it follow the eyes is to want what one sees and act on it; the law warns against the same thing (Numbers 15:39). This takes up the eyes of verse 1.

decisions.choice: a blemish: a stain of guilt
decisions.reason: The word (mum, here spelled with an extra letter) is a flaw or blemish. On the hands it is the guilt of wrong done with them, such as violence or dishonest gain; Job said there is no violence on his hands (16:17).

decisions.choice: whatever my eyes wanted; of wrongdoing
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what the pictures mean (m2, m3).

records.source: אֶ֭זְרְעָה וְאַחֵ֣ר יֹאכֵ֑ל וְֽצֶאֱצָאַ֥י יְשֹׁרָֽשׁוּ׃
records.gloss: Let me sow, and another eat, and my produce let them be rooted up.
pieces: then let me sow and another eat, \q and let my crops be uprooted.

L.8: let me sow and another eat, \q and let my produce be rooted out.

R.8: If I have, then let me plant and let someone else eat. \q Let my crops be pulled up by the roots.

decisions.choice: let me sow: the curse that completes the oath of verse 7
decisions.reason: Here Job speaks the curse on himself (see verse 5). It fits the wrong: if his hands took what was not theirs, let others take what his hands have sown.

decisions.choice: sowing for someone else: the curse of wasted labor
decisions.reason: The law and the prophets name this curse on the disobedient: to plant and have another eat it (Leviticus 26:16; Deuteronomy 28:30, 33; Micah 6:15). Eliphaz had said the same would happen to the fool (5:5); Job swears it may happen to him if he is guilty.

decisions.choice: my produce: my crops
decisions.reason: The word (tse'etsa'im) means "what comes out": crops from the ground or children from a family. Job uses it of descendants elsewhere (21:8; 27:14). Here sowing and rooting up point to crops, as in Isaiah 34:1 and 42:5 of what the earth brings forth; but it could also mean "my descendants".

decisions.choice: then
decisions.reason: Balanced adds "then" to mark where the curse begins after the long "if" clause.

decisions.choice: If I have, then
decisions.reason: Readable asks its questions first (verse 5, r-en-1), so it introduces the curse with "If I have, then".

records.source: אִם־נִפְתָּ֣ה לִ֭בִּי עַל־אִשָּׁ֑ה וְעַל־פֶּ֖תַח רֵעִ֣י אָרָֽבְתִּי׃
records.gloss: If has been enticed my heart by a woman, and at [the] door of my neighbor I have lain in wait,
pieces: If my heart has been lured by a woman, \q or I have lurked at my neighbor's door,

L.9: If my heart has been enticed by a woman, \q and at my neighbor's door I have lain in wait,

R.9: Have I let a woman lead me astray? \q Have I hidden near my neighbor's door, waiting for his wife?

decisions.choice: enticed: drawn into sin by desire
decisions.reason: The verb (patah) means to be persuaded or seduced, foolishly drawn in. It comes again in verse 27, of being drawn into idolatry. Proverbs uses the picture of the young man led astray by another man's wife (Proverbs 7:21-22).

decisions.choice: lain in wait at my neighbor's door: waited for the husband to leave in order to commit adultery
decisions.reason: To lie in wait at a neighbor's door is to watch for the time the husband is away, to go in to his wife. Job had described the adulterer who waits for the dusk (24:15); compare Proverbs 7:8-12. The woman in the first line is the neighbor's wife.

decisions.choice: waiting for his wife
decisions.reason: Readable says what the waiting at the door is for (m2).

records.source: תִּטְחַ֣ן לְאַחֵ֣ר אִשְׁתִּ֑י וְ֝עָלֶ֗יהָ יִכְרְע֥וּן אֲחֵרִֽין׃
records.gloss: Let grind for another my wife, and over her let bow down others.
pieces: then let my wife grind grain for another man, \q and let other men lie with her.

L.10: let my wife grind for another, \q and let others kneel over her.

R.10: If I have, then let my wife grind grain as a servant for another man, \q and let other men sleep with her.

decisions.choice: grind for another: become another man's servant
decisions.reason: Grinding grain with a hand mill was the lowest work of the house, done by servant women (Exodus 11:5; Isaiah 47:2). Job's wife would become someone else's servant. The word may also hint at the sexual meaning of the next line, so that both lines say she would belong to another man.

decisions.choice: kneel over her: have sexual relations with her
decisions.reason: To bend or kneel over a woman is a plain picture of sexual intercourse.

decisions.choice: the curse matches the crime
decisions.reason: If Job had taken another man's wife, let his own be taken from him. The ancient household was one unit, so the punishment of the head of the house fell on the whole house (compare 2 Samuel 12:11). Job does not wish this on his wife; he names it as the worst he can think of, to show how sure he is of his innocence.

decisions.choice: lie with her (B), sleep with her (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the picture means (m2); Literal keeps "kneel over her".

decisions.choice: grain; another man; as a servant (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable supply "grain" and "man" (the Hebrew "another" is masculine); Readable adds "as a servant" for the first meaning of grinding (m1).

records.source: כִּי־הִ֥יא זִמָּ֑ה וְ֝ה֗וּא עָוֺ֥ן פְּלִילִֽים׃
records.gloss: For that [is] lewdness, and it [is] an iniquity [for] judges.
pieces: For that would be a shameful crime, \q a wrong to be punished by the judges.

L.11: For that [is] lewdness, \q and it [is] an iniquity [for] judges.

R.11: That would be a terrible sin, \q a crime that judges should punish.

decisions.choice: lewdness: a deliberately wicked, shameful act
decisions.reason: The word (zimmah) is used especially of sexual wickedness (Leviticus 18:17; 20:14; Judges 20:6).

decisions.choice: an iniquity for judges: a crime for the courts to punish
decisions.reason: Adultery was not only a private sin but a crime that the law punished, with death (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22). The same phrase comes again of idolatry in verse 28.

decisions.choice: that: the pronoun as it is read (feminine)
decisions.reason: The written Hebrew text has the masculine pronoun "he/it" here, and the traditional reading notes say to read the feminine "she/it", which agrees with the feminine noun that follows. Both mean "that", so the sense does not change.

decisions.choice: would be
decisions.reason: Hebrew has no verb here. Balanced and Readable supply "would be", since Job is speaking of something he did not do.

records.source: כִּ֤י אֵ֣שׁ הִ֭יא עַד־אֲבַדּ֣וֹן תֹּאכֵ֑ל וּֽבְכָל־תְּב֖וּאָתִ֣י תְשָׁרֵֽשׁ׃
records.gloss: For a fire it [is] that to Abaddon devours, and in all my produce it would root out.
pieces: It is a fire that burns all the way to Abaddon, \q and it would root out all my harvest.

L.12: For it [is] a fire that devours as far as Abaddon, \q and it would root out all my harvest.

R.12: It is like a fire that burns all the way down to the place of destruction. \q It would destroy everything I have.

decisions.choice: Abaddon: the place of destruction, the realm of the dead
decisions.reason: Abaddon means "destruction" and is a name for the world of the dead, set beside Sheol (26:6; 28:22; Proverbs 15:11). The fire of adultery burns all the way down to death itself.

decisions.choice: adultery as a fire
decisions.reason: Proverbs uses the same picture: a man cannot carry fire in his lap and not be burned, and the one who goes in to his neighbor's wife will not go unpunished (Proverbs 6:27-29). The sin destroys the one who commits it and everything he has (Proverbs 5:9-10).

decisions.choice: root out all my harvest: destroy all I have gained
decisions.reason: "Root out" repeats the curse of verse 8. The harvest stands for all the fruit of a lifetime's work.

decisions.choice: is like a fire; the place of destruction; everything I have
decisions.reason: Readable marks the picture as a comparison, renders Abaddon "the place of destruction" as elsewhere in Job, and says what the harvest stands for (m3).

records.source: אִם־אֶמְאַ֗ס מִשְׁפַּ֣ט עַ֭בְדִּי וַאֲמָתִ֑י בְּ֝רִבָ֗ם עִמָּדִֽי׃
records.gloss: If I rejected [the] cause of my male slave and my female slave in their complaint with me,
pieces: If I have refused justice to my male or female servants \q when they brought a complaint against me,

L.13: If I have rejected the cause of my male slave or my female slave \q when they brought a complaint against me,

R.13: Have I refused to give my servants, men or women, a fair hearing \q when they had a complaint against me?

decisions.choice: male slave, female slave: servants Job owned
decisions.reason: The words ('eved, 'amah) name servants who belonged to their master, not hired workers. They had little power to bring a case against him. Job swears that he still heard their complaints as one party heard another, though they were his property; that is the force of the next two verses.

decisions.choice: cause, complaint: a legal claim
decisions.reason: The words (mishpat, riv) belong to the law court: a person's rightful case and the dispute brought. Job treated his servants' grievances as real cases, to be judged fairly.

decisions.choice: slave (L), servants (B, R)
decisions.reason: As elsewhere, Literal says "slave" and Balanced and Readable "servant", with m1 recording that they were owned. The point here is the fairness Job showed, not slavery set against freedom, so the usual rule applies.

records.source: וּמָ֣ה אֶֽ֭עֱשֶׂה כִּֽי־יָק֣וּם אֵ֑ל וְכִֽי־יִ֝פְקֹ֗ד מָ֣ה אֲשִׁיבֶֽנּוּ׃
records.gloss: And what would I do when rises God? And when he visits, what would I answer him?
pieces: what would I do when God rises up? \q When {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} calls me to account, what answer would I give {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}?

L.14: what then would I do when God rises up? \q And when {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} calls [me] to account, what would I answer {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}?

R.14: If I had, what could I do when God stands up to judge me? \q What could I say when {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} asks me to explain?

decisions.choice: God rises up: God stands up as judge
decisions.reason: To "rise up" is what a judge does to give judgment (Psalm 76:10; 82:8). Job imagines God taking his servants' side against him.

decisions.choice: visits: examines, calls to account
decisions.reason: The verb (paqad) means to visit or inspect, and often to look into someone's conduct in order to punish (7:18; Psalm 17:3).

decisions.choice: God: the word 'El
decisions.reason: Job uses the short name 'El, rendered "God".

decisions.choice: If I had; to judge me; asks me to explain
decisions.reason: Readable links this to its question in verse 13 and says what rising up and visiting mean (m1, m2).

records.source: הֲֽ֝לֹא־בַ֭בֶּטֶן עֹשֵׂ֣נִי עָשָׂ֑הוּ וַ֝יְכֻנֶ֗נּוּ בָּרֶ֥חֶם אֶחָֽד׃
records.gloss: Not in the womb the one making me made him? And fashioned us in the womb one?
pieces: Did not the one who made me in the womb make them too? \q Did not the same God form us both in the womb?

L.15: Did not the one who made me in the womb make him? \q And did not one fashion us in the womb?

R.15: God made me before I was born, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} made my servants too. \q The same God formed every one of us in the womb.

decisions.choice: the same Maker: master and servant are equal before God
decisions.reason: Job's reason for hearing his servants is that God made both of them. Proverbs draws the same conclusion about the poor (Proverbs 14:31; 22:2), and Malachi asks, "Has not one God created us?" (Malachi 2:10).

decisions.choice: one: the one God who formed us
alternatives: formed us in the same way in the womb
decisions.reason: The last word ("one") can be the subject, the one God who shaped both master and servant, or it can go with "womb": "in one womb", meaning in the same way. Read as the subject it echoes "the one who made me" in the first line.

decisions.choice: them too; my servants (R)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew "him" means the servant of verse 13, man or woman. Balanced says "them" and Readable "my servants", so the line covers both.

decisions.choice: the same God
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable take "one" as God (m2) and say so.

records.source: אִם־אֶ֭מְנַע מֵחֵ֣פֶץ דַּלִּ֑ים וְעֵינֵ֖י אַלְמָנָ֣ה אֲכַלֶּֽה׃
records.gloss: If I withheld from [the] desire of [the] poor, and [the] eyes of [the] widow I caused to fail,
pieces: If I have refused the poor what they longed for, \q or let the widow's eyes grow weary with waiting,

L.16: If I have withheld from the poor [what they] desired, \q or caused the eyes of the widow to fail,

R.16: Have I ever refused to give poor people what they needed? \q Have I let a widow look for help until she gave up hope?

decisions.choice: caused the eyes of the widow to fail: let her look for help in vain
decisions.reason: Eyes "fail" when they have looked for something so long that they grow dim and the hope is gone (11:20; 17:5; Lamentations 4:17).

decisions.choice: the poor and the widow: an answer to Eliphaz
decisions.reason: Eliphaz had accused Job of sending widows away empty and crushing orphans (22:6-9). Verses 16-22 answer that charge point by point. The law sets the poor, the widow and the orphan under God's protection (Exodus 22:21-23; Deuteronomy 24:17-22).

decisions.choice: one long oath, verses 16-22
decisions.reason: The "if" clauses run from verse 16 to verse 21, with verse 18 set in between, and the curse comes in verse 22.

decisions.choice: what they needed
decisions.reason: Readable says "needed" for what the poor longed for, since what they wanted was the means to live.

records.source: וְאֹכַ֣ל פִּתִּ֣י לְבַדִּ֑י וְלֹא־אָכַ֖ל יָת֣וֹם מִמֶּֽנָּה׃
records.gloss: And I ate my morsel by myself, and not ate [the] orphan from it,
pieces: or eaten my bread alone, \q and not shared it with the orphan,

L.17: and have eaten my morsel by myself, \q and the orphan has not eaten from it,

R.17: Have I eaten my food alone \q and not shared it with orphans?

decisions.choice: my morsel by myself: my food without sharing it
decisions.reason: "Morsel" (pat) is a piece of bread, an ordinary meal. To eat it alone, when the hungry are near, is to refuse the duty of sharing food (Isaiah 58:7; Proverbs 22:9).

decisions.choice: orphan: a fatherless child
decisions.reason: The word (yatom) is a child without a father, who had no one to provide or speak for him; the mother may still be living.

decisions.choice: not shared it with the orphan
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "not shared" for "the orphan has not eaten from it", the same act seen from Job's side.

records.source: כִּ֣י מִ֭נְּעוּרַי גְּדֵלַ֣נִי כְאָ֑ב וּמִבֶּ֖טֶן אִמִּ֣י אַנְחֶֽנָּה׃
records.gloss: For from my youth he grew up with me as [with] a father, and from [the] womb of my mother I guided her,
pieces: for from my youth the orphan grew up with me as with a father, \q and from my mother's womb I have guided the widow;

L.18: for from my youth he grew up with me as [with] a father, \q and from my mother's womb I have guided her;

R.18: In fact, since I was young I have raised orphans like a father. \q All my life I have guided widows.

decisions.choice: he grew up with me: the orphan grew up in Job's care; her: the widow
alternatives: he (God) brought me up as a father
decisions.reason: The verse breaks into the oath to say that the opposite was true: "he" is the orphan of verse 17 and "her" the widow of verse 16. The first verb, as written, reads "he grew up with me" or "he brought me up"; the second fits Job raising the orphan as a father would. Some read the first line with a small change of vowels as "I brought him up", which gives the same sense.

decisions.choice: from my youth, from my mother's womb: all my life
decisions.reason: "From my mother's womb" is an overstatement meaning "for as long as I have lived" (Psalm 22:11; 71:6). Job says caring for the helpless has always been his way.

decisions.choice: the orphan, the widow
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the orphan and the widow for "he" and "her" (m1), so the reader is not left to guess who is meant. Readable makes the verse a separate statement.

records.source: אִם־אֶרְאֶ֣ה א֭וֹבֵדמִבְּלִ֣י לְב֑וּשׁ וְאֵ֥ין כְּ֝ס֗וּת לָאֶבְיֽוֹן׃
records.gloss: if I saw [one] perishing for lack of clothing, and there was no covering for the needy,
pieces: if I have seen anyone dying for lack of clothing, \q or the needy with nothing to cover them,

L.19: if I have seen [anyone] perishing for lack of clothing, \q or the needy without covering,

R.19: Have I seen anyone dying because they had no clothes, \q or a poor person with nothing to keep them warm?

decisions.choice: perishing: in danger of dying, here from cold
decisions.reason: The verb ('avad) means to perish. Without a cloak the poor could die of cold in the night; Job himself had described them lying naked with no covering in the cold (24:7), and Eliphaz had accused him of stripping the naked (22:6). The law forbade keeping a poor man's cloak overnight (Exodus 22:25-26).

decisions.choice: the needy: a poor person without means
decisions.reason: The word ('evyon) is someone in want, who depends on others for help.

decisions.choice: anyone ... them
decisions.reason: The Hebrew words are masculine but mean any person in need, man or woman, so Balanced and Readable say "anyone" and "them".

records.source: אִם־לֹ֣א בֵרֲכ֣וּנִי חֲלָצָ֑יו וּמִגֵּ֥ז כְּ֝בָשַׂי יִתְחַמָּֽם׃
records.gloss: if not blessed me his loins, and from [the] fleece of my lambs he warmed himself,
pieces: if their bodies have not blessed me \q because they were warmed with the fleece of my sheep,

L.20: if his loins have not blessed me, \q and he has not warmed himself with the fleece of my lambs,

R.20: Have I failed to give them warm wool from my sheep, \q so that they had no reason to bless me?

decisions.choice: blessed: thanked and spoke well of
decisions.reason: Here "bless" is real blessing: the poor man thanks Job and asks God's good on him (29:13). It is not the euphemism for "curse" of 1:5.

decisions.choice: his loins have blessed me: his warmed body was itself a thanks
decisions.reason: The loins (the waist and hips, the body's middle) stand for the whole body, now clothed. Job speaks as if the warmed body itself gave thanks.

decisions.choice: if not: an oath that Job did clothe them
decisions.reason: "If ... not" in an oath means "I swear that I did" (see verse 5). Job swears that the poor were clothed by him and blessed him for it.

decisions.choice: their bodies
decisions.reason: Balanced says "bodies" for "loins" (m2) and "they" for the poor of verse 19, men or women. Literal keeps "his loins".

decisions.choice: Have I failed to give them ... so that they had no reason to bless me?
decisions.reason: Readable keeps its question form (verse 5, r-en-1), and turns "if they have not blessed me" into the failure it would imply.

records.source: אִם־הֲנִיפ֣וֹתִי עַל־יָת֣וֹם יָדִ֑י כִּֽי־אֶרְאֶ֥ה בַ֝שַּׁ֗עַר עֶזְרָתִֽי׃
records.gloss: if I have raised against [the] orphan my hand, because I saw in the gate my help,
pieces: if I have raised my hand against the orphan \q because I saw I had support at the city gate,

L.21: if I have raised my hand against the orphan, \q because I saw my help in the gate,

R.21: Have I ever threatened an orphan \q because I knew the judges at the city gate would take my side?

decisions.choice: raised my hand against: threatened or attacked
decisions.reason: To wave or raise the hand against someone is to threaten them with violence (Isaiah 11:15; 19:16), here a helpless child with no father to defend him.

decisions.choice: help in the gate: support in the court
decisions.reason: The city gate was where the elders sat to judge cases (Deuteronomy 21:19; Ruth 4:1-2). Job had sat there among the leaders (29:7). He swears he never used that standing to win against an orphan.

decisions.choice: threatened; the judges at the city gate would take my side
decisions.reason: Readable says what the raised hand and the help in the gate mean (m1, m2).

records.source: כְּ֭תֵפִי מִשִּׁכְמָ֣ה תִפּ֑וֹל וְ֝אֶזְרֹעִ֗י מִקָּנָ֥ה תִשָּׁבֵֽר׃
records.gloss: My shoulder from its shoulder let it fall, and my arm from its socket let it be broken.
pieces: then let my shoulder fall from its blade, \q and let my arm be broken off at the socket.

L.22: let my shoulder fall from its shoulder blade, \q and let my arm be broken from its socket.

R.22: If I have, then let my arm fall off my shoulder, \q and let it be broken off at the joint.

decisions.choice: the curse matches the crime
decisions.reason: The arm raised against the orphan (verse 21) is the one Job asks to be broken. Later God says that the raised arm of the wicked is broken (38:15).

decisions.choice: shoulder, shoulder blade, socket
decisions.reason: The first word (katef) is the shoulder, the second (shekhem) the upper back where the shoulder joins it. The last word (qaneh) means "reed" or "stalk", here the upper arm bone or the joint where it fits; either way the arm is torn from the body.

decisions.choice: then
decisions.reason: Balanced marks the start of the curse after the long "if" clauses of verses 16-21.

decisions.choice: If I have, then
decisions.reason: Readable gives the curse after its questions (verse 5, r-en-1).

records.source: כִּ֤י פַ֣חַד אֵ֭לַי אֵ֣יד אֵ֑ל וּ֝מִשְּׂאֵת֗וֹ לֹ֣א אוּכָֽל׃
records.gloss: For [a] terror to me [was the] calamity of God, and because of his majesty not I could.
pieces: For I dreaded disaster from God, \q and because of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} majesty I could not do such things.

L.23: For calamity from God [was] a terror to me, \q and because of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} majesty I could not [do so].

R.23: I was afraid of the disaster God would send. \q God is so great that I could never do such things.

decisions.choice: calamity from God: the ruin God sends on the wicked
decisions.reason: This is the same word as in verse 3 ('eyd): the disaster God sends on the unjust. Job kept from those wrongs because he feared it.

decisions.choice: his majesty: God's exalted greatness
decisions.reason: The word (se'et) means being lifted up, God's overwhelming majesty. Job had warned the friends that God's majesty would terrify them (13:11).

decisions.choice: I could not: I could not do such things
decisions.reason: The Hebrew stops at "I could not". Most naturally Job means he could not do the wrongs he has listed; it might also mean he could not stand before God's majesty.

decisions.choice: God: the word 'El
decisions.reason: 'El, rendered "God", as in verse 14.

decisions.choice: do such things
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable complete the short Hebrew phrase as m3 reads it; Literal brackets "do so".

records.source: אִם־שַׂ֣מְתִּי זָהָ֣ב כִּסְלִ֑י וְ֝לַכֶּ֗תֶם אָמַ֥רְתִּי מִבְטַחִֽי׃
records.gloss: If I have made gold my confidence, and to fine gold I have said, "My trust,"
pieces: If I have put my confidence in gold, \q or said to fine gold, "You are my security,"

L.24: If I have made gold my confidence, \q or said to fine gold, "My trust,"

R.24: Have I trusted in gold? \q Have I said to pure gold, "You keep me safe"?

decisions.choice: gold, fine gold
decisions.reason: The second word (ketem) is a poetic word for the purest gold (28:16, 19). The two lines say the same thing twice.

decisions.choice: confidence, trust in wealth: a kind of idolatry
decisions.reason: To rely on wealth for safety is to put it where God belongs (Psalm 52:9; Proverbs 11:28). Verses 24-27 hold two oaths, against trusting wealth and against worshiping the sun and moon, and verse 28 gives one verdict on both: denying God.

decisions.choice: confidence: what one relies on
decisions.reason: The word (kesel) is what a person trusts in; Bildad used it of the wicked man's false hope (8:14).

records.source: אִם־אֶ֭שְׂמַח כִּי־רַ֣ב חֵילִ֑י וְכִֽי־כַ֝בִּ֗יר מָצְאָ֥ה יָדִֽי׃

pieces: if I have rejoiced because my wealth was great, \q because my hand had gained so much,

L.25: if I have rejoiced because my wealth was great, \q and because my hand had found much,

R.25: Have I been happy because I was so rich, \q because I had earned so much?

decisions.choice: my hand had found much: I had gained a great deal
decisions.reason: For the hand to "find" is to acquire or be able to get (Leviticus 12:8; Isaiah 10:14).

decisions.choice: rejoicing in wealth as one's security
decisions.reason: Job had been very rich (1:3). The wrong is not in owning wealth but in taking joy in it as if it were one's life (Psalm 62:11).

decisions.choice: gained (B), earned (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "my hand had found" means (m1).

records.source: אִם־אֶרְאֶ֣ה א֖וֹר כִּ֣י יָהֵ֑ל וְ֝יָרֵ֗חַ יָקָ֥ר הֹלֵֽךְ׃
records.gloss: if I saw [the] light when it shone, and [the] moon splendid going,
pieces: if I have looked at the sun when it shone, \q or the moon moving in its splendor,

L.26: if I have looked at the light when it shone, \q or the moon moving in splendor,

R.26: Have I looked up at the shining sun \q or the bright moon moving across the sky,

decisions.choice: the light: the sun
decisions.reason: Set beside the moon, "the light" is the sun (as in 37:21 and Genesis 1:16, "the greater light").

decisions.choice: looking at sun and moon: being drawn to worship them
decisions.reason: Worship of the sun and moon was common in the ancient world, and Israel's law forbade it (Deuteronomy 4:19; 17:3; 2 Kings 23:5; Ezekiel 8:16). "Looked at" here is the gaze of admiration that leads to worship, as verse 27 shows.

decisions.choice: the sun
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "sun" for "the light" (m1); Literal keeps "the light".

records.source: וַיִּ֣פְתְּ בַּסֵּ֣תֶר לִבִּ֑י וַתִּשַּׁ֖ק יָדִ֣י לְפִֽי׃
records.gloss: and was enticed in secret my heart, and kissed my hand to my mouth,
pieces: and my heart has been secretly enticed, \q so that I threw them a kiss with my hand,

L.27: and my heart has been secretly enticed, \q and my hand has kissed my mouth,

R.27: and been secretly tempted to worship them? \q Have I blown them a kiss with my hand?

decisions.choice: my hand has kissed my mouth: a kiss thrown as an act of worship
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says the hand kissed (or was kissed) at the mouth: the worshiper kissed his hand and held it out toward the sun or moon. Kissing was a gesture of worship toward idols (1 Kings 19:18; Hosea 13:2).

decisions.choice: secretly enticed: privately drawn in
decisions.reason: The same verb as in verse 9 (patah). Even a hidden, inward turning to the heavenly lights would be a betrayal of God (verse 28).

decisions.choice: threw them a kiss (B), blown them a kiss (R)
alternatives: my hand has kissed my mouth
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say in English what the gesture was (m1); Literal keeps "my hand has kissed my mouth".

decisions.choice: tempted to worship them
decisions.reason: Readable says what the heart was enticed to do (m2; verse 26, m2).

records.source: גַּם־ה֭וּאעָוֺ֣ן פְּלִילִ֑י כִּֽי־כִחַ֖שְׁתִּי לָאֵ֣ל מִמָּֽעַל׃
records.gloss: Also that [is an] iniquity [for] judges, for I would have denied God from above.
pieces: this too would be a crime to be punished by the judges, \q for I would have been false to God above.

L.28: that also [would be] an iniquity [for] judges, \q for I would have denied God above.

R.28: If I had, that would be a crime that judges should punish. \q I would have turned my back on God in heaven.

decisions.choice: an iniquity for judges: a crime for the courts
decisions.reason: The phrase is the same as in verse 11, with an adjective form of the word for judges. Worship of other gods was a crime under the law (Deuteronomy 17:2-7).

decisions.choice: denied: been false to, disowned
decisions.reason: The verb (kichesh) means to deny or deal falsely with someone (Joshua 24:27; Proverbs 30:9). Trusting in gold or worshiping the sky would disown God, who is above all of them.

decisions.choice: God: the word 'El
decisions.reason: 'El, rendered "God".

decisions.choice: If I had; turned my back on
decisions.reason: Readable gives the verdict after its questions (verse 5, r-en-1) and says "turned my back on" for "denied" (m2).

records.source: אִם־אֶ֭שְׂמַח בְּפִ֣יד מְשַׂנְאִ֑י וְ֝הִתְעֹרַ֗רְתִּי כִּֽי־מְצָ֥אוֹ רָֽע׃
records.gloss: If I rejoiced at [the] ruin of [one] hating me, and I roused myself when found him evil,
pieces: If I have rejoiced at the ruin of someone who hated me, \q or gloated when disaster overtook them,

L.29: If I have rejoiced at the ruin of one who hated me, \q or exulted when evil found him,

R.29: Have I been glad when someone who hated me was ruined? \q Have I gloated when trouble came to them?

decisions.choice: not rejoicing over an enemy's fall
decisions.reason: Proverbs forbids gloating when an enemy falls (Proverbs 24:17), and the law commands help for an enemy's animal (Exodus 23:4-5). Job swears that he kept even his heart free of such joy.

decisions.choice: exulted: was roused to glee
decisions.reason: The verb ('ur, in a reflexive form) means to stir oneself up, here to be excited with delight.

decisions.choice: if without a curse: an oath that he did not
decisions.reason: No curse follows this "if"; verse 30 breaks in instead. As in verse 5, "if" in an oath then means "I swear I did not".

decisions.choice: someone ... them
decisions.reason: The enemy may be anyone, so Balanced and Readable say "someone" and "them"; Literal keeps "him".

records.source: וְלֹא־נָתַ֣תִּי לַחֲטֹ֣א חִכִּ֑י לִשְׁאֹ֖ל בְּאָלָ֣ה נַפְשֽׁוֹ׃
records.gloss: And not have I given to sin my palate, by asking with a curse his life.
pieces: I have not let my mouth sin \q by calling down a curse on their life.

L.30: And I have not let my palate sin \q by asking for his life with a curse.

R.30: No, I have never let my mouth sin \q by cursing them and wishing them dead.

decisions.choice: Job breaks into the oath with a plain statement
decisions.reason: Instead of a curse on himself, Job states outright that he has not done it, and goes further: he did not even speak against the enemy.

decisions.choice: palate: mouth, speech
decisions.reason: The palate stands for what one says (6:30; Proverbs 8:7).

decisions.choice: asking for his life with a curse: wishing him dead with a spoken curse
decisions.reason: A curse ('alah) was a spoken call for harm. To "ask for his life" by it is to call down death on him (compare 1 Kings 3:11).

decisions.choice: mouth; their (B), them (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "mouth" for "palate" (m2), and keep the enemy of verse 29 as "them".

records.source: אִם־לֹ֣א אָ֭מְרוּ מְתֵ֣י אָהֳלִ֑י מִֽי־יִתֵּ֥ן מִ֝בְּשָׂר֗וֹ לֹ֣א נִשְׂבָּֽע׃
records.gloss: If not have said [the] men of my tent, "Who can give from his meat [one] not satisfied?"
pieces: If the {{gender:people|men}} of my household have not said, \q "Who has not had their fill of his meat?"

L.31: If the men of my tent have not said, \q "Who can find [one] not filled with his meat?"

R.31: The {{gender:people|men}} of my household have always said, \q "Everyone has eaten all the meat they wanted at Job's table."

decisions.choice: if not: an oath that they did say it
decisions.reason: As in verse 20, "if ... not" in an oath means "I swear that it is so": the people of Job's house did say this.

decisions.choice: who can give one not filled: there is no one who has not been fed
alternatives: Oh that we had some of his meat!
decisions.reason: The question "who can give (that is, find) someone not filled with his meat?" means that everyone was fed. Meat was a sign of a generous table, since most people ate it rarely. Verse 32 gives the same picture of hospitality.

decisions.choice: the men of my tent: the members of my household
decisions.reason: The word (metim) means men, people. "My tent" is Job's household, its servants and dependants, as in 19:15 and 29:4.

decisions.choice: people / men of my household
decisions.reason: The household who spoke would have been men and women, so Balanced and Readable use the gender setting; Literal keeps "men", the word's own meaning.

decisions.choice: have always said; a statement in place of the question; Job's table
decisions.reason: Readable gives the plain meaning of the oath and the question (m1, m2), and names Job for "his" since the quoted words speak of him.

records.source: בַּ֭חוּץ לֹא־יָלִ֣ין גֵּ֑ר דְּ֝לָתַ֗י לָאֹ֥רַח אֶפְתָּֽח׃
records.gloss: In the street not lodged a sojourner; my doors to the traveler I opened.
pieces: No outsider had to spend the night in the street, \q for I opened my doors to the traveler.

L.32: The sojourner did not lodge in the street; \q I opened my doors to the traveler.

R.32: No stranger ever had to sleep outside in the street. \q I always opened my doors to travelers.

decisions.choice: hospitality to the stranger
decisions.reason: A traveler with nowhere to stay spent the night in the town square unless someone took him in (Genesis 19:2; Judges 19:15-21). Job swears that no one in his town ever had to.

decisions.choice: the traveler: the same consonants as "the path", read with different vowels
alternatives: I opened my doors to the road
decisions.reason: The vowels in the Hebrew text give "to the path" ('orach). The same letters read 'oreach mean "traveler", which fits the parallel with "sojourner", as the ancient translations understood it.

decisions.choice: sojourner: a foreigner living or staying away from home
decisions.reason: The word (ger) is someone from elsewhere, without land or family to protect him.

decisions.choice: sojourner (L), outsider (B), stranger (R)
decisions.reason: The usual renderings of ger in this translation; Readable "stranger" suits a traveler who has just arrived.

records.source: אִם־כִּסִּ֣יתִי כְאָדָ֣ם פְּשָׁעָ֑י לִטְמ֖וֹן בְּחֻבִּ֣י עֲוֺֽנִי׃
records.gloss: If I have covered like humankind my transgressions, by hiding in my bosom my iniquity,
pieces: If I have concealed my transgressions as people do, \q by hiding my guilt in my heart,

L.33: If I have covered my transgressions like humankind, \q by hiding my iniquity in my bosom,

R.33: Have I hidden my sins the way people do, \q keeping my guilt a secret?

decisions.choice: like humankind: as people commonly do
decisions.reason: The word ('adam) can mean "humankind" or be the name Adam. As people do, Job could have hidden his faults; or he may mean "like Adam", who hid from God after his sin (Genesis 3:8-12).

decisions.choice: transgressions, iniquity: wrongs and the guilt for them
decisions.reason: The first word (pesha') is rebellion, breaking faith; the second ('avon) is wrongdoing and the guilt it brings. Job does not claim to be sinless (7:21; 13:26); he swears that he never hid what he did wrong.

decisions.choice: in my bosom: inside, out of sight
decisions.reason: The bosom (chov) is the inside of the garment at the chest, where something is kept hidden; it also stands for the inner self.

decisions.choice: my guilt in my heart
decisions.reason: Balanced says "guilt" for the iniquity one carries and "heart" for the bosom as the inner self (m2, m3).

records.gloss: because I dreaded [the] great multitude, and [the] contempt of clans terrified me, and I kept silent, not I went out [the] door,
pieces: because I feared the great crowd \q and the contempt of the clans terrified me, \q so that I kept quiet and would not go out of my door—

L.34: because I dreaded the great multitude, \q and the contempt of clans terrified me, \q so that I kept silent and did not go out the door—

R.34: Was I so afraid of what the crowd would say, \q so scared that the families around me would despise me, \q that I kept quiet and stayed inside?

decisions.choice: the crowd, the contempt of clans: public disgrace
decisions.reason: Job pictures the shame a man would face if his hidden sin became known to the town and its families. He had been honored at the gate (29:7-10); he swears he never hid wrongdoing to keep that honor.

decisions.choice: dreaded, terrified: deep fear
decisions.reason: The first verb ('arats) means to tremble at, the second (chatat) to be shattered with fear.

decisions.choice: the oath breaks off
decisions.reason: The oath of verses 33-34 has no curse. Job breaks off and cries out for a hearing (verse 35), and the last oath and its curse come in verses 38-40.

decisions.choice: a dash that leads into verse 35
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced end the verse with a dash, since the oath has no curse and Job breaks off into his cry in verse 35 (m3).

records.source: מִ֤י יִתֶּן־לִ֨י׀שֹׁ֘מֵ֤עַֽ לִ֗י הֶן־תָּ֭וִי שַׁדַּ֣י יַעֲנֵ֑נִי וְסֵ֥פֶר כָּ֝תַ֗ב אִ֣ישׁ רִיבִֽי׃
records.gloss: Who will give to me [one] hearing me! Here [is] my mark; let Shaddai answer me! And [the] document [that] has written [the] man of my case!
pieces: Oh, that I had someone to hear me! \q Here is my signature; let the Almighty answer me! \q If only I had the charge my accuser has written!

L.35: Oh that I had one who would hear me! \q Here [is] my mark; let the Almighty answer me! \q And [oh for] the document my opponent at law has written!

R.35: I wish someone would listen to me! \q I have signed my name to all I have said. Now let God All-Powerful answer me! \q Let the one who accuses me write down the charges against me!

decisions.choice: who will give: oh that, if only
decisions.reason: "Who will give ...?" is the Hebrew way of saying "if only" (6:8; 14:4; 23:3). Job used it when he wished his words were written in a document (19:23); now he wants the charges against him written.

decisions.choice: my mark: my signature
decisions.reason: The word (taw) is the name of the last letter of the Hebrew alphabet, which in old script was a cross-shaped mark (Ezekiel 9:4, 6). Here it is the mark a man puts to a document as his signature. Job signs his oath of innocence and hands it to the court.

decisions.choice: the man of my case: my opponent at law; most likely God himself
decisions.reason: "The man of my case" is the other party in a lawsuit. Job has asked God to state his charges (10:2; 13:22-23; 23:3-7), so the opponent is most likely God, whom he has just asked to answer; it could be any accuser. The text does not name him.

decisions.choice: the document: the written indictment
decisions.reason: A written document (sefer) could be a legal record, such as a certificate of divorce (Deuteronomy 24:1). Here it is the list of charges. Job is sure it would clear him (verse 36).

decisions.choice: I have signed my name to all I have said; God All-Powerful
decisions.reason: Readable says what the mark is and what it is put to (m2), and names Shaddai "God All-Powerful", as in every book.

decisions.choice: the charge (B), the charges (R); my accuser
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the document is (m4) and use "accuser" for "the man of my case", which keeps open who he is (m3).

records.source: אִם־לֹ֣א עַל־שִׁ֭כְמִי אֶשָּׂאֶ֑נּוּ אֶֽעֶנְדֶ֖נּוּ עֲטָר֣וֹת לִֽי׃
records.gloss: If not on my shoulder I would carry it; I would bind it [as] crowns on me.
pieces: I would surely carry it on my shoulder; \q I would wear it like a crown.

L.36: Surely on my shoulder I would carry it; \q I would bind it on me [as] a crown.

R.36: I would proudly carry it on my shoulder. \q I would wear it on my head like a crown.

decisions.choice: if not: surely
decisions.reason: "If not" is the form of an oath meaning "surely, I swear I would" (see verse 5).

decisions.choice: carry it on my shoulder, bind it on as a crown: display it openly, with honor
decisions.reason: Far from hiding the charges in shame (contrast verses 33-34), Job would wear them in public like a badge of honor, sure they would prove his innocence. The word for crown is plural (as in Zechariah 6:11), perhaps a crown made of several rings.

decisions.choice: proudly; on my head
decisions.reason: Readable makes plain that carrying it would be a sign of honor (m2).

records.source: מִסְפַּ֣ר צְ֭עָדַי אַגִּידֶ֑נּוּ כְּמוֹ־נָ֝גִ֗יד אֲקָרֲבֶֽנּוּ׃
records.gloss: [The] number of my steps I would declare to him; like a prince I would approach him.
pieces: I would give {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} an account of every step I have taken; \q like a prince I would come near to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

L.37: The number of my steps I would declare to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}; \q like a prince I would approach {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.37: I would tell {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} everything I have done. \q I would walk up to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} like a prince.

decisions.choice: the number of my steps: answers verse 4
decisions.reason: Job asked whether God does not count all his steps (verse 4). Now he offers to give the count himself, a full account of his life.

decisions.choice: a prince: a leader, a man of rank
decisions.reason: The word (nagid) is a ruler or leader. Job would come before his judge with his head up, not as a guilty man cowering.

decisions.choice: him: the opponent of verse 35, most likely God
decisions.reason: The pronoun refers back to "the man of my case" in verse 35, read there as God (verse 35, m3).

decisions.choice: deity pronoun for him
decisions.reason: Since verse 35 reads Job's opponent as God, the pronouns take the deity pronoun setting; if he is another accuser, they would be plain "him".

records.source: אִם־עָ֭לַי אַדְמָתִ֣י תִזְעָ֑ק וְ֝יַ֗חַד תְּלָמֶ֥יהָ יִבְכָּיֽוּן׃
records.gloss: If against me my land cries out, and together its furrows weep,
pieces: If my land has cried out against me, \q and its furrows have wept together,

L.38: If my land cries out against me, \q and its furrows weep together,

R.38: Has my land cried out against me? \q Have its plowed fields wept because of me?

decisions.choice: the land cries out: the land itself as a witness to wrong
decisions.reason: The ground cried out over Abel's blood (Genesis 4:10-11), and stones and beams cry out against those who build by violence (Habakkuk 2:11). Land taken unjustly or worked by oppressed laborers would cry out against its owner.

decisions.choice: the last oath
decisions.reason: After his signature (verse 35) Job makes one more oath, with its curse, about how he got and used his land. With it his speech ends.

decisions.choice: plowed fields; because of me
decisions.reason: Readable says "plowed fields" for "furrows" and supplies the reason they weep.

records.source: אִם־כֹּ֭חָהּאָכַ֣לְתִּי בְלִי־כָ֑סֶף וְנֶ֖פֶשׁ בְּעָלֶ֣יהָ הִפָּֽחְתִּי׃
records.gloss: If its strength I have eaten without silver, and [the] life of its owners I have caused to breathe out,
pieces: if I have eaten its yield without payment, \q or made its owners breathe their last,

L.39: if I have eaten its strength without silver, \q or caused the life of its owners to breathe out,

R.39: Have I eaten its crops without paying for them? \q Have I caused the death of the people it belonged to?

decisions.choice: its strength: what the land produces
decisions.reason: The land's "strength" (koach) is its yield, as in Genesis 4:12, where the ground will no longer give Cain its strength.

decisions.choice: made its owners breathe out their life: caused their death
decisions.reason: To make the life "breathe out" is to bring someone to their last breath. Job would have taken the land by killing or ruining its rightful owners, as Ahab did Naboth (1 Kings 21). The phrase could also mean making them gasp in despair (11:20; Jeremiah 15:9), or the owners could be the tenants who worked the land.

decisions.choice: without silver: without paying
decisions.reason: Silver was the money of the ancient world. To eat the produce without silver is to take it without paying the owner or the workers (Jeremiah 22:13).

decisions.choice: yield, crops; without payment
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the land's strength and the silver mean (m1, m3).

records.source: תַּ֤חַת חִטָּ֨ה׀יֵ֥צֵא ח֗וֹחַ וְתַֽחַת־שְׂעֹרָ֥ה בָאְשָׁ֑ה תַּ֝֗מּוּ דִּבְרֵ֥י אִיּֽוֹב׃פ
records.gloss: Instead of wheat let come up thorns, and instead of barley foul weeds. Are ended [the] words of Job.
pieces: then let thorns grow instead of wheat, \q and foul weeds instead of barley. \q The words of Job are ended.

L.40: instead of wheat let thorns come up, \q and instead of barley foul weeds. \q The words of Job are ended.

R.40: If I have, then let thorns grow instead of wheat, \q and stinking weeds instead of barley. \q This is the end of Job's words.

decisions.choice: thorns instead of wheat: the curse on the ground
decisions.reason: Job calls on his land the curse of Genesis 3:17-18, thorns in place of grain. If he had wronged the land, let it fail him.

decisions.choice: foul weeds: stinking weeds
decisions.reason: The word (bo'shah) comes from a verb meaning "to stink"; it names some foul-smelling weed whose kind is not known (compare the "stinking" wild grapes of Isaiah 5:2, 4).

decisions.choice: The words of Job are ended: a closing note
decisions.reason: These words close Job's speeches to his friends, like the note "The prayers of David son of Jesse are ended" with the same verb (Psalm 72:20). Job speaks again only briefly in answer to God (40:3-5; 42:1-6).

decisions.choice: then
decisions.reason: Balanced marks the start of the curse after the "if" clauses of verses 38-39.

decisions.choice: If I have, then; stinking weeds; This is the end of Job's words
decisions.reason: Readable gives the curse after its questions (verse 5, r-en-1), says "stinking weeds" (m2), and puts the closing note in plain words.
